summary: IMAP normally makes a client wait for a server continuation request before sending literal string data. This standards-track RFC specifies an alternate non-synchronizing literal form that avoids that network round trip, defining two IMAP extensions.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking Can I send now and waiting for a yes, you just send it, saving a back-and-forth.

questions: what is the difference between literal+ and literal-
subtitle: Lets IMAP clients send string data without waiting for the server's go-ahead, saving a network round trip.

tldr.problem: IMAP requires a client sending a literal to wait for a server command continuation request after the octet count and before the string data, which costs a network round trip.
tldr.mechanism: A non-synchronizing literal puts a plus sign before the closing brace, such as {11+}, so the client can send the octets at once. LITERAL+ allows this everywhere, and LITERAL- allows it only for literals of 4096 bytes or less.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2088 and registers LITERAL- as a new capability. Servers must not advertise both capabilities.

today: RFC 7888 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2016. It obsoletes RFC 2088 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Problem with Synchronizing Literals
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol (RFC 3501) has a syntactic construct called a literal for sending strings. When a client sends one, IMAP requires it to wait for a command continuation request from the server between the octet count and the string data.

This document defines an alternate form that avoids that round trip, and specifies two IMAP extensions, LITERAL+ and LITERAL-. It obsoletes RFC 2088.
sections.eli5: It is like having to ask 'ready?' and wait for 'yes' before handing over every note. This RFC lets you skip the asking.

sections.title: The Non-synchronizing Literal
sections.content:
A non-synchronizing literal has a plus (+) between the octet count and the closing brace. The original form is called a synchronizing literal. The new form MUST NOT be sent from server to client.

A client may use it only when the server lists LITERAL+ or LITERAL- in its CAPABILITY response. The server does not send a continuation request, and the client need not wait before sending the octets.

The server MUST check the end of every received line for an open brace, an octet count, a plus and a close brace right before the CRLF. The literal is not delimited by CRLF: it ends after the stated number of bytes, and the command continues from there. A space needed between parameters must appear after the literal.

A server MAY still process commands and reject errors line by line, as long as it checks for non-synchronizing literals at the end of each line.
sections.eli5: A plus sign in the size tag means 'I am just sending it, no need to reply first'. The server counts the bytes and keeps going.

sections.title: Example: LOGIN
sections.content: The RFC shows a LOGIN command written with two non-synchronizing literals. It is semantically equivalent to one that uses quoted strings, and the space after FOOBAR in the first version corresponds to the space between the two quoted strings in the second.
sections.eli5: Sending the user name and password with tags that say how long each is gives the same result as writing them in quotes.

sections.title: LITERAL- and the 4096-Byte Limit
sections.content:
Non-synchronizing literals can be hard on servers. If a client sends one that is too big, a LITERAL+ server has two poor choices. It can read all the bytes and reject the command anyway, which wastes bandwidth, though it may send the tagged BAD or NO response before reading the whole literal. Or it can send an untagged BYE and close the connection, which can leave naive clients reconnecting and repeating the operation in an infinite loop.

The problem is most common with APPEND. So LITERAL- is almost identical to LITERAL+, except that non-synchronizing literals MUST NOT be larger than 4096 bytes. Larger ones MUST be sent as synchronizing literals. The form still uses the plus sign.

If a LITERAL- server answers an oversized APPEND with a tagged BAD, it MUST include the TOOBIG response code. With an untagged BYE it SHOULD include it. Servers MUST NOT advertise both capabilities at the same time.

The RFC also points to the APPENDLIMIT extension (RFC 7889), which lets a server advertise its APPEND limit so that well-behaved clients avoid uploading big messages.
sections.eli5: Sending without asking is fine for small notes, but a huge parcel might not fit. LITERAL- says to skip the asking only for notes up to 4096 bytes.

sections.title: Interaction with BINARY and MULTIAPPEND
sections.content:
RFC 4466 updated the literal8 syntax from RFC 3516 to allow non-synchronizing literals when both BINARY and LITERAL+ are supported. This document allows the same extended syntax when BINARY and LITERAL- are both supported.

RFC 3502 describes MULTIAPPEND and how it works with LITERAL+. LITERAL- can be used with MULTIAPPEND in the same way.
sections.eli5: The new, smaller-limit version works with the other IMAP add-ons the same way the first one did.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Non-synchronizing literals can consume extra resources, such as memory, on IMAP servers and can be used for denial-of-service attacks. The LITERAL- extension partially improves this. Some servers limit the literals they accept, and generally can set much lower limits for commands other than APPEND.

Otherwise the document raises no security concerns beyond those of RFC 3501.
sections.eli5: Someone could flood a server with huge packages it has to hold. A size cap helps keep that in check.
